name: もつ鍋と焼酎のお店 とうか (Touka (Motsunabe to Shochu no Mise Touka))

claims.text: Menu includes fried squid karaage and fried gyoza dumplings, both typically using wheat-based coatings/wrappers; no dedicated gluten-free fryer or preparation area was mentioned in any source.

The motsunabe hot pot broth is offered in five flavors including soy sauce, miso, and pork bone; standard Japanese soy sauce and miso contain wheat, and no wheat-free tamari alternative was mentioned.
The menu centers on wagyu beef offal, shabu-shabu meats, raw ham, and smoked duck; no vegetarian or vegan dishes were identified in any source, and hot-pot broths are meat-based.

name: つけ麺 ズッパ 水道橋店 (Tsukemen Zuppa (Suidobashi))

claims.text: The base menu already excludes meat and fish across every dish, using soy "meat" and soy milk instead of animal protein and dashi, so there is no shared meat/fish cooking line to cross with a vegan order.

Vegan modifications — such as leaving the boiled egg off the tsukemen set, or preparing the soy-milk tantanmen without the pungent alliums — are made to order once you tell staff after buying your ticket at the vending machine.
The kitchen uses no meat or fish anywhere on the menu; soup and toppings are vegetable- and soy-protein-based throughout, marketed as guilt-free even if you finish the dipping broth.
Described as Suidobashi's only vegan-focused tsukemen and ramen shop, popular with vegan and vegetarian diners including foreign tourists.

name: つけそば 神田 勝本 (Tsukesoba Kanda Katsumoto)

claims.text: The dipping broth's tare is a shoyu (soy sauce) base, per the menu item 清湯（しょうゆ）つけそば, served with wheat noodles; no gluten-free noodle alternative is offered.
The dipping broth is built from niboshi (dried sardines), other dried-fish stocks, and chicken (including Nagoya Cochin), with no vegetable-only broth option documented.

name: つるとんたん UDON NOODLE Brasserie 渋谷店 (TsuruTonTan UDON NOODLE Brasserie Shibuya)

claims.text: The noodle broth is a shoyu (soy sauce) base and the noodles are standard wheat udon, made fresh at each location — wheat is present throughout the core menu.

The signature dashi is built from Hokkaido Rishiri kombu and Kagoshima Makurazaki bonito (fish) flakes, and is used as the base for most dishes on the standard menu, including many vegetable-topped bowls, so most dishes are not vegan by default.
Table-side ordering tablets support English, Korean, and Chinese, which can make it easier to ask staff about ingredients even without shared Japanese.

name: 梅園 浅草本店 (Umezono Asakusa Honten)

claims.text: Umezono is not listed among FindMeGlutenFree's Taito City / celiac-friendly gluten-free spots; the dedicated GF option celiacs cite in Asakusa is Tempura Asakusa Sakura, not Umezono — indicating no celiac community recognition of Umezono as GF-safe.

Menu confirms the same kitchen makes wheat-batter dorayaki (どら焼) and matcha/soft-serve dora items alongside the naturally wheat-free sweets, establishing on-site wheat-flour handling and cross-contact exposure.

Shop and aggregator pages surface no allergen table or gluten-free statement for Umezono; Japanese search for '梅園 浅草 アレルギー表示 グルテンフリー 対応' returns no shop allergen info, only unrelated fully-GF venue まるごとVeganダイニング浅草.

Anmitsu is described as served with agar (kanten), sweet bean paste, shiratama, and vanilla ice cream — confirming the default anmitsu is NOT vegan (dairy) while the jelly component is plant-based agar rather than gelatin.

name: ヴィーガン イート トウキョウ (Vegan Eat Tokyo)

claims.text: Described in multiple listings as a fully vegan kitchen (French-chef-supervised, organic, plant-based menu) with no animal products on the menu, which by design limits vegan cross-contact risk, though no explicit cross-contact protocol statement was found.

Listed as a certified vegan restaurant recognized by NPO Veg Project Japan, and highly rated (around 4.7/5 on Google Maps as of late 2024) by a large volume of international visitors via the HappyCow app.

name: ヴィーガン居酒屋 真さか (Vegan Izakaya Masaka)

claims.text: Every dish on the menu is made using only plant-derived ingredients — the kitchen does not use meat, fish, dairy, or eggs at all, which removes the risk of animal-product cross-contact that vegan diners would face in a mixed kitchen.
The restaurant is listed on WE TABLE, a Tokyo guide specifically curating restaurants that accommodate food allergies and special diets.
Also listed on Vegewel, a dedicated vegetarian/vegan/gluten-free restaurant directory for Japan.

name: VEGEGO MIYASHITA PARK（ベジゴー ミヤシタパーク） (VEGEGO MIYASHITA PARK)

claims.text: No source discusses gluten-free cross-contamination practices; the kitchen is a small food-court stall serving fried chicken and standard Korean seasonings alongside everything else, so unconfirmed contact with wheat-based items should be assumed.

The signature bibimbap is built on a base of housemade namul (seasoned vegetables) and mixed grains, giving a genuinely vegetable-heavy option on the menu compared with a typical Korean BBQ restaurant.
